newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Defence urges delay in Rwanda genocide trial.
newsitem.headline: Defence urges delay in Rwanda genocide trial.

text.p: The defence lawyer for a Rwandan on trial for genocide threatened on Thursday to resign unless the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda granted a postponement.
Johan Scheers, Belgian defence lawyer for Rwandan Hutu Jean Paul Akayesu, also asked the Arusha tribunal to release the accused until trial. The court said it would decide on Friday.
"I asked the tribunal to postpone his case," Scheers told reporters after presenting motions in court. "I am not ready to plead...I asked the court to release him (until his trial)."

Akayesu, 43, was brought to court in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha in handcuffs but was released before entering the courtroom and sat attentive in a dark blue suit and tie but looking slightly nervous during two court sessions on Thursday.
Earlier on Thursday in the first session open to the media since May, the court agreed to prosecution requests to protect witnesses by keeping their identity from the public and media.
If the defence request for a postponement is accepted on Friday it will be the second trial delay ordered in three days after the first defendent charged received a delay on health grounds.

Asked what would happen if the three-judge court decided Akayesu's trial went ahead as scheduled immediately, Scheers said: "I leave. I resign...I am not defending anybody without reading the testimony of the (prosecution) witnesses."
He said a new defence attorney would have to be appointed.

Scheers said immediately after Thursday's court session the prosecutor told him he had just sent the defence 800 pages of prosecution witness testimony. The defence lawyer said if this was true he still needed at least two months to prepare a case.

"Today was one of the hardest things I have ever had to do. It is not pleasant standing up there and saying what I said against the tribunal," added Scheers, who says he been unable to find any of the up to 40 defence witnesses named by Akayesu.
He said Akayesu told him he preferred to stay in jail in Arusha and go to trial with a full defence than continue on Thursday, the trial date set when he pleaded not guilty in May.

On Wednesday, the court postponed the trial of Georges Rutaganda, 38, from October to next March because he is seriously ill but refused to release him. His defence lawyer said unless the defendent received treatment he would die before trial.
Judge Navanethem Pillay of South Africa said on Thursday the court accepted a prosecution motion for the identity of witnesses in Rutaganda's case to be kept secret from the public for their safety.

In particular, the court ordered that the names, addresses and the whereabouts and other identifying data should not be divulged to the public, media or the defence until they were "brought under the protection" of the tribunal in Arusha.
Witnesses would testify using pseudonyms and no photographs or sketches of them would be permitted, the court ordered.

Prosecuting attorney Yakob Haile Mariam said witnesses were warned friends or associates of Rutaganda woull seek revenge on them and their families if they appeared. He said the house of one witness was set ablaze and she had received death threats.

Akayesu was bourgmestre or the local government leader in Rwana's Taba commune in the three-month genocide and is charged with failing to stop killings, inciting the public to slaughter, hunting down minority Tutsis and ordering killings.
The tribunal has been dogged by delays, poor communications from its base in this northern Tanzanian farming town and the vast problem of finding who was responsible for the genocide.
It has indicted only 21 suspects and has only three in detention, charged with crimes against humanity and genocide.
